# pwpush Call Relationships

`lib/tasks/pwpush.rake` remains the starting point for reading the rake side of pwpush. After review, the draft's note to "read from the top all the way to the exit" is retained as a reading-order hint, but is no longer treated as an execution chain. This file contains the rake module's definition context, task declarations, and task bodies. These sections sit next to each other in the file, but address different questions when reading the code.

Start at the top. Loading, visible constants, and helper objects are prerequisites for defining the tasks. They allow rake to load this file or make the declarations that follow valid. The relationship here should be recorded as "visible before definition," not "already called during task execution." If a task is not recognized, the file fails to load, or a declaration does not appear, this is the section to revisit. Connecting such a case directly to actions in the task body would mix the loading phase with the execution phase.

Next, confirm the module scope and task declarations. A declaration gives rake an entry-point name, but the name alone does not tell us how much the task body will do. After a declaration, the body might only prepare arguments, or it might immediately hand off control; conditional branches may also prevent some actions from happening at all. Task declarations are therefore useful for marking "where to enter," but cannot stand in for the call relationships that follow. Review notes should first record the declaration's location, then look for direct actions in each task's own body, to avoid incorrectly attributing everything in the same file to a single task execution.

```text
lib/tasks/pwpush.rake
  ├─ rake module and top-level dependencies
  ├─ Task declarations
  │    └─ Direct calls in the task body
  │         ├─ Conditional branches or early exits
  │         ├─ Failure leaving the task body
  │         └─ Event exit points
  └─ Subsequent handling outside the file
```

The hierarchy in the diagram marks review locations; it is not a runtime sequence diagram. Top-level dependencies are visible before task definition, but do not necessarily appear in every execution. Direct calls in the task body are the handoffs that can be explicitly traced from this file. "Outside the file" at the bottom only means that control has left `lib/tasks/pwpush.rake`; it does not supply names for any services, consumers, or error handlers.

The draft grouped all "objects that appear in the file" as called objects. That classification is not sufficient. They are now recorded in two categories: top-level objects under the definition context, and objects explicitly referenced in the task body on execution edges. On review, this lets us first determine whether an object is needed when the file is loaded or is only reached after the task is triggered. Both kinds of relationship are worth retaining, but they should not be drawn as one line.

The locations of branches in the task body must also be retained. A call inside a condition only means it may happen when that condition is met. An action before an early exit does not mean a later exit point has been reached. At such a location, record the call, the branch it belongs to, and whether control remains in this file afterward. Do not use "the task will call" to turn a conditional edge into a required edge, and do not treat an early exit as an exception exit.

The end of the file is the second place where distinct cases are easily conflated. At least two cases need to be kept apart here: failure leaving the task body, and the task emitting an event after completing its local actions. In the first case, check whether the same file already contains actions that catch, transform, or rethrow the failure. If not, stop at the point where it leaves. In the second case, record only which section of the task body emits the event. An event having been emitted does not mean consumption outside the file has completed, nor does it mean subsequent actions succeeded.

This distinction is useful when investigating. If the task cannot be loaded, first revisit the top-level dependencies, module scope, and declarations. If an error occurs after the task has entered its body, work backward from the last visible direct call to inspect conditions and early exits. If the event chain is in question, leave this file at the emission point and continue tracing. All three starting points relate to pwpush, but they should not share one generic "task failure" record.

During review, read backward from the end to confirm exit points. First find the last action still visible in the task body, then check whether any branches, early exits, or points that hand failure back to rake precede it. This avoids assuming that top-level dependencies are also part of task cleanup simply because they were encountered first. If the end is an event exit point, mark the extent of the task body before that exit. If it is a failure leaving the task, mark the last visible location within this file. Both records provide a precise starting point for opening downstream code and continuing the trace.

This page does not provide an overview of implementations outside the file. If the task body hands off to another rake task, this page retains only the handoff location and the name of the task it hands off to. That task's internal behavior should be examined at its own source location. Likewise, consumption, notification, or recording after an event exit point must wait for confirmation in subsequent files before being added. Inserting downstream details into this page prematurely would obscure the actual clues provided by `lib/tasks/pwpush.rake`: where it defines the entry point and where it hands off control.

The notation we can continue using is to attach every relationship to a location in the file and label it as part of the definition context, a task declaration, a task-body action, an action inside a condition, or a final exit point. There is no need to repeat the same edge across multiple paragraphs. If actual task declarations or direct calls are added in the next update, insert them at their corresponding locations rather than mixing top-level dependencies, runtime actions, and handling outside the file back into a single section.

Putting event exits last in the rereading order does not mean they necessarily execute last. An event exit is simply a marker that requires tracing back: when you reach a location that sends an action outward, return to the local section that triggers it. The old diagram placed "Failures" and "Events" on adjacent lines, which led people to read them as naturally connected. There was no evidence for that connection; they are now examined independently. Whether they fall on the same local path must still be determined by the actual conditions within the file.

The reading order now used is:

```text
Declarations within the file
   ↓
First use of direct dependencies
   ↓
Exit points of failure branches
   ↓
Trigger points for event exits
```

This sequence diagram specifies only how to read the file after opening it; it does not assert any complete runtime model for the controller. In particular, it avoids two old misreadings: inferring that the entry point is unique from the directory name, and inferring a fixed order between "Failures" and "Events" because they are adjacent. The former was withdrawn in the second review; the latter was also dropped after the reading checkpoints were distinguished again.

When tracing back through the code, you can first make two independent marks within the controller: one for the section containing the declarations and one for the first appearance of the dependencies. Then record failure exits only when you encounter a branch exit; do not classify every return location as the same kind of failure handling. For event-related code, likewise record only the trigger location. Until you have returned to the local handling, do not label it a success notification, a failure notification, or any fixed outcome. Taking notes this way is slower, but it keeps the three kinds of locations most easily confused in their original context.

No interface fields, request parameters, or response shapes have been added here, because those details fall outside the verification scope already covered by this entry-point record. The controller path and the four reading checkpoints are still enough to support later navigation. More detailed object relationships must be added when the original file is opened, not inferred from this page's old diagram.

Items still missing:

- The actual object names declared within the file and the sections containing them;
- The handling branch containing the first appearance of each direct dependency;
- The local actions before and after each failure exit;
- The trigger conditions for event exits;
- Whether an event exit overlaps with a failure exit.

This page therefore retains a starting point for reading the code, with its revision history visible. To locate push handling for API v1, start with the file and the four reading checkpoints. To determine what a particular event means, you cannot keep relying on the original diagram that placed the exits next to each other.

# Response Security and Offline Asset Decisions

In the hardening discussion for 2.3.0, two browser-side concerns need to be recorded separately first: the security restrictions sent with the page response, and whether frontend scripts can be fetched without connecting to external resources. Both become visible only after the user opens the page, so early investigations often treated them as one issue. At this point, we don't think the same implementation location should be responsible for both.

The initial working assumption was to handle page security centrally where responses are generated, and to start the offline work by checking whether the required scripts had been included in the local directory. That assumption was useful for finding entry points, but "the file exists" is not yet proof that the browser can resolve the module. The browser also goes through module names and mappings; neither had been checked at the time.

The old search notes left `vendor/javascript/clipboard.js` here. It came up because of terms such as clipboard, self, and base, which makes it easy to conflate scripts, clipboard capabilities, and page permissions. At this stage, treat this path only as a starting point for frontend asset context. The path name alone does not establish that it generates page responses, nor that it determines offline loading.

There were four options on the table at the time: add restrictions to individual pages, or handle them centrally at the response layer; define offline support as vendor files having been delivered, or as module names resolving to local files. The comparison of the first two is not finished; the latter two should no longer be conflated. Follow-up review should examine page responses and module resolution relationships separately.

For this decision, whether a page displays camera or clipboard controls is not yet a criterion for judging the security policy. Controls, script calls, and response content are different observation points. Conversely, the existence of a local script does not establish that the offline entry point is complete.

To confirm: whether the clipboard-related scripts in the old references are only page functionality dependencies or also connect to the module-loading entry point; and whether page restrictions are generated in one shared location or are also added by individual pages.

# Decision on Response Security and Offline Assets

Following this review, the early claim that "offline assets only need to be in the vendor directory" must remain on record as written, but can no longer serve as a criterion. Files in a directory tell us where they are delivered; the name the browser uses to request a module, whether that name is mapped, and whether the mapped target can be retrieved are separate matters. The old claim has not been deleted because it explains why early investigations often stopped once the files were found.

## Starting with the Combined Issue

The brief note from 2023 classified both response security and offline assets as browser-side issues. That approach had the advantage of fewer starting points: looking at the page and then the frontend files seemed enough to cover the same set of anomalies. The review found that this classification conflated response behavior at the end of a request with loading behavior after the page starts parsing modules.

A page response is the result returned by a request. By the time the browser receives the page, the headers have already arrived with the response. Offline module loading happens as the page continues parsing frontend modules: the browser needs a module name, and that name must resolve to a target in the deliverables. Both paths can make it look as though "something is wrong with the page," but neither is a subsequent step of the other.

The first version listed four directions: add restrictions locally in the page, handle responses centrally, check vendor files, and check the relationship between module names and files. No complete decision was made on any of them at the time. The only explicit point was that the page security policy should not be inferred directly from the name of `vendor/javascript/clipboard.js`. That qualification is still useful, since the path can indeed lead readers back to the old frontend asset context.

## Counterexamples Raised in Review

The most useful counterexample in the review discussion was simple: a local file can exist without the page using it under a resolvable name. Conversely, a page response that looks normal on one occasion does not mean offline modules will necessarily reach the browser. The original "single page check" therefore cannot establish conclusions for both issues.

This does not mean directory checks are useless. If the target asset is missing, the name and mapping naturally have nothing to point to; that is simply a fact about the assets. The problem is recording that fact as proof that offline loading is complete. A file existing, a name existing, and a name mapping to the correct target are different checks. A break in any one of them can change what the browser actually loads.

Likewise, whether a page has a visible entry point for a capability is not enough to establish what restrictions its response carries. The UI may have no camera entry point while the response may still need to express limits on browser capabilities. Clipboard-related behavior on a page also does not mean a script name can substitute for inspecting the response content. The early practice of treating page functionality as the scope of the policy was narrowed after this discussion.

## Two Records

After the review, the checks were split into two records. The first records only what was observed in the page response, without drawing further inferences from the JavaScript path. The second records only the relationship between module names, mappings, and local assets, without drawing further inferences from page headers. They may come from the same regression run or appear in the same release batch, but their results should be recorded separately.

This separation does not require a complete table for every vendor file. Only when offline module loading is in question do the name, mapping, and local target all need to be investigated. Ordinary frontend scripts should not automatically be brought within the offline boundary unless they are part of that question.

The place of `vendor/javascript/clipboard.js` in these records is also clearer. It is still a file likely to turn up through the old search entry points, and inspecting it may help explain the frontend context at the time. It is not, however, evidence of page security restrictions. The similarity between clipboard in the path and the browser's clipboard capability does not mean the file is where response headers are defined. That association can help start a search; it cannot justify stopping one.

## Provisional Plan (Retained)

> For offline mode, first check for the target script in the image; finding the file is enough to consider it available offline. Page security is determined by whether the page uses the camera or clipboard.

This passage reflects the original intent of the early plan and no longer applies. The first sentence confuses an asset's presence in the image with the browser's ability to resolve a module. The second mistakes visible functionality for the sole scope of response policy. It is retained not for continued execution, but to explain why the check order was later changed.

The replacement working rule is: for offline issues, first distinguish assets, module names, and mappings; for response issues, first observe the page response. When both change in the same version, their respective results can be stored alongside each other, but they cannot share a single conclusion that "the page opens." A restriction may still be absent even when the page opens; a page can also carry the expected headers while a required module name still has no local target.

## A Recheck That Could Not Be Combined

Someone tried using the same page sample to answer both lines of inquiry. That approach did not yield a reusable basis for judgment. Inspecting the response could establish what that request returned, but not how all module assets resolved. Checking local files could establish that the target was included, but not whether the response was generated from a centralized location. After the recheck, the combined sample was retained only as background, no longer as a shared format for making both assessments.

This recheck also surfaced two interpretations of the "offline asset boundary": one meant that remote resources should not be requested; the other meant that all vendor files had to be available. Both claims go beyond the available material. The discussion here is limited to the relationship between the module names required by the page, their mappings, and the corresponding local assets. It does not extend to all static resources or establish conclusions about container preparation or the release process.

## Provisional Decision

The decision is to keep response security and offline assets in the same historical record because both came from the same round of hardening for 2.3.0, but no longer tie them together under a single implementation responsibility or a single rationale for checks. The page response is verified by observing the response. Offline modules are verified through the relationship between names, mappings, and local assets.

The next review only needs to address two focused questions: whether references in the old search entry points still explain the frontend asset relationships in use, and whether page restrictions are generated from a stable location. The former will not establish a conclusion for the latter. The latter will not prove that module names correctly resolve to local targets either.
versions.change_summary: Keep the legacy approach and review the two categories of items separately

# Response Security and Offline Asset Decision

This record began as a consolidated note before release. Later addenda did not erase the earlier statements, but appended each newly discovered counterexample. The resulting text is not very tidy, but it shows why the issues were repeatedly misjudged: some people traced script names to permissions, some stopped after finding files in local directories, and others treated whether a page displayed a particular control as the scope of the response policy.

This page addresses the relationship between response security policy and offline asset boundary in 2.3.0 cumulative hardening. Both concern the browser, but they cannot be assessed using the same object. Audit page navigation and theme mode are adjacent topics and are not included in this decision.

## 2023: The Initial Combined Framing

The initial description was brief: "Review browser-side security and offline resources together." Its mistake was not putting both matters into the same release cycle, but describing two different objects of observation as the same thing.

The page response has already been formed by the time the request returns. When the browser receives the page, the response headers arrive at the same time. Offline module loading happens after the page continues parsing modules: the browser needs to know the module name and resolve that name to an asset it can retrieve. Both paths may ultimately manifest as abnormal page behavior, but they are not successive steps in a single chain.

The convenient check at the time was to first confirm that the target script existed in the vendor directory, then check whether the page used the related functionality. This method had practical value: it could quickly locate the frontend context and rule out cases where something had clearly not been included in the deliverable. Its shortcomings only became apparent later. A file in the directory only establishes the asset side of things; it does not establish what name the browser uses to look for it, much less whether the page will resolve that name to that file.

The old search records retained `vendor/javascript/clipboard.js`. In early searches starting with terms such as clipboard, self, and base, this path often appeared first. The path was therefore retained as an entry point back to the frontend asset context at the time. It was not an example casually added to the text, and it should not be deleted; however, a filename resembling a browser capability does not mean that it produced the restrictions in the page response.

The first draft presented four directions: add browser restrictions on individual pages, or handle them centrally where responses are generated; interpret offline support as local files having been delivered, or as module names being resolvable to local files. The first version did not conflate these four options into a single decision. Only one thing was settled at that point: do not treat the JavaScript path as the place responsible for the response policy merely because its name resembles a permission term.

Two questions also remained at the time. Were the clipboard-related scripts merely dependencies for page functionality, or did they also feed into the module-loading entry point; were page restrictions generated in one stable location, or added separately by each page. There was not enough material to answer these questions early on, so the path was not elevated to evidence of the policy.

## A Review Addendum: First Clarify What Is Being Examined

Later reviews did not initially argue about whether browser capabilities should be restricted, but about how the restrictions should be identified. One view held that when the page does not display camera or clipboard controls, there is no need to include the related capabilities in the response. Another view held that controls are facts at the UI layer, while the page response is the object that needs to be checked separately.

This disagreement did not end immediately because the offline assets had not been clearly separated either. If it is not even clear where the frontend modules come from, attributing every browser issue to the page layer will only turn a single investigation into a mixture of two conclusions. The interim approach after the review was to keep two separate records: one documenting what was actually observed in the page response, and the other documenting the relationships among module names, local assets, and mappings.

These two records may come from the same regression run, but each answers only its own question. The response record cannot show whether a given module can be resolved offline; the asset record cannot show what restrictions a particular page response carried. This separation adds descriptive detail, but avoids the leap that "the script was found, so the page policy has taken effect."

One reminder was also retained from the review: starting the investigation from `vendor/javascript/clipboard.js` is not unreasonable, as it can lead to early frontend clues; but it should be treated as a starting point for retrieval, not as the answer. Even if new reference relationships are found later, they will only describe how the file is used in its surrounding context and cannot replace observing the page response.

## 2024 Review: File existence does not mean loading succeeds

During the second pass, the most useful counterexample was straightforward. A local file may already be included in the deliverable, while the page does not use it under a resolvable name; conversely, the restriction in the page response may be correct, while the module name still does not resolve to a local target. The previous approach of using the same page sample to prove both things therefore could not reach a conclusion.

From this point on, the offline portion was split into two observation areas. The asset side asks whether the target JavaScript is retained as a local file. This question cannot be omitted, because without the asset, the subsequent mapping has nothing to point to. The resolution side asks what name the page uses when referencing the module, whether that name has a mapping, and whether the file indicated by the mapping can be fetched by the browser. The former is not a shorthand for the latter.

This separation also explains two different types of failure. When the asset is local but the name is missing, the directory check will pass, while module resolution may still fail; when the name and mapping exist but the target asset is missing, the page may already know what it needs to look for, yet still have no usable content. From the user's perspective, both situations look like "the frontend did not load normally," but the locations for the subsequent checks are different.

Response security follows the same observation principle, but with a narrower object: do not infer from buttons, page styles, or script filenames; instead, inspect the browser's page response. This does not deny that frontend code is related to security, but puts the final behavior back where the browser actually received it. The absence of a capability entry somewhere on the page does not automatically mean that the response has no restriction; the presence of related functionality on the page does not automatically mean that the restriction comes from that functionality's script.

During the review, some people interpreted the offline asset boundary as "no remote requests allowed," while others interpreted it as "all vendor files must be available." Both claims go beyond the existing material. The narrower boundary used here is the relationship among the module names the page needs, the importmap mappings for those names, and the local assets those mappings point to. It does not count all ordinary static resources as modules, nor does it infer complete requirements for the container or release process from this page.

## The old approach remains in place

The following preserves the original intent of an early approach, now deprecated:

> In offline mode, check the local directory first; having the target script in the directory is sufficient. Page security is determined by page functionality; unused capabilities do not need to be represented in the response.

The problem with the first sentence is not that checking the directory is wrong, but that it was mistaken for a complete conclusion. A file being in the vendor directory means the deliverable includes it; this does not answer whether the page imports it under the corresponding name, or whether a mapping points that name to the file. The problem with the second sentence is that it conflates capabilities visible in the user interface with response policy. The two may be related, but neither can substitute for the other.

This passage was not rewritten into the later, correct formulation so as to preserve why the investigation at the time stopped at "the file exists," and why some people followed clipboard-related scripts in search of page restrictions. The old steps can explain the history, but are no longer used to assess current changes.

Another old simplification was: as long as the same page opens, mark both the security headers and offline loading as working correctly. The actual review showed that this statement did not distinguish enough between the two. A page may open while a particular browser restriction is not returned as expected; a page may also carry the expected policy while a required module name still has no local target. Being able to open is an observation, not a shared basis for assessing these two issues.

## An experiment record

One round of review deliberately used the same page sample for both types of assessment. First, the content returned by the page was inspected, and then the local assets were checked. The results did not establish a reusable conclusion that "both pass": inspecting the response only showed the restrictions for that particular page request; inspecting the local file only showed that the file was included in the deliverable. Whether the module name was correct, whether a mapping existed, and where the mapping ultimately led were not automatically answered by using the same sample.

What this result changed was not the implementation, but the way findings were recorded. Afterward, "the page works" was no longer written as a combined result for the two tracks. For responses, record the response itself; for offline modules, record the relationship among names, mappings, and assets. When both appear in the same release batch, their results can be stored next to each other without letting one serve as approval for the other.

The experiment also exposed a common association. On seeing the word clipboard, readers tend to treat `clipboard.js`, browser clipboard writes, and response security restrictions as sharing the same implementation location. This association helps with searching old material, but is not suitable for determining ownership. The file may merely be a dependency of a page feature, or it may only provide some frontend behavior; in either case, its name alone cannot be used to infer the HTTP response.

## Trade-offs after the meeting

Someone then proposed continuing to trace through the old file and determining all page policies along the way. This proposal was not adopted. The reason was not that the path was irrelevant, but that it belonged to the frontend asset context, while the location where responses are generated is a different category of object. Following the file further might yield clues about calls, or it might yield only vendor clues; neither result can replace inspecting the page response.

Another simplification that was not adopted was defining offline support as "the file exists in the image". This can quickly filter out obviously missing assets, but it misses issues such as names without mappings or mappings that point to different targets. Therefore, the presence of a file in the directory is retained only as an asset-side check, and is no longer treated as a passing condition for offline module loading.

A brief comment from the meeting was later kept in the margin: first clarify whether you are looking at a response or resolution, then decide which file to inspect. It is not a broad workflow, but a constraint against repeating an earlier misjudgment. Response issues should first return to the page response; module issues should first return to names, mappings, and target assets. The two lines of investigation can meet, but neither should bear responsibility for the other's conclusions.

## Consolidation Before the Current Decision

At this stage, four facts can be reliably distinguished, none of which can substitute for another: whether the page returned security restrictions; whether a particular frontend file is in the local deliverables; whether the browser module name is recognized by the importmap; and whether the recognized name points to an accessible local asset.

These four items do not all need to be rechecked for every change. If the change concerns page restrictions, first verify the page response. If the change concerns an offline module entry point, first verify the module name, mapping, and local asset. When both types of changes are in the same version, save the observations side by side. This is to avoid incorrect attribution, not to consolidate all browser behavior into a single implementation point.

The note on the old path is also narrowed here. `vendor/javascript/clipboard.js` can still help return to the original frontend context, but its name cannot establish the specific content of clipboard restrictions, nor can its local presence establish the state of the importmap. If troubleshooting starts from this file, continue until the current reference relationships are found; do not treat finding the path itself as a decision.

The current entry point for verifying offline modules is `config/importmap.rb`. It provides the pins needed for browser module resolution. For the Popper ESM asset, the module name is `@popperjs/core`, and the local target remains at `vendor/javascript/@popperjs--core--esm.js`. The three are the name, mapping, and asset, respectively; confirming only one of them should not lead to recording offline loading as established.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Page response
    Page response --> Response restrictions
    [*] --> Module name
    Module name --> importmap mapping
    importmap mapping --> Local asset
```

The two starting points in the diagram are deliberately not connected. Page responses and module resolution occur in the same browser session, but the available material does not support drawing them as a single execution chain. The diagram also does not depict the clipboard file as a policy node; it remains only an entry point for historical lookup.

## Decision for the Current Version

Browser responses preserve the Feature-Policy compatibility header and the Permissions-Policy header, including camera 'none', camera=(), clipboard-write=(self), and the same-origin base-uri directive. The Content-Security-Policy script-src uses a per-response nonce and strict-dynamic; consecutive responses must not reuse a nonce.

This requirement applies to browser page responses, not to a particular JavaScript file, and does not depend on whether the page displays camera or clipboard controls. The compatibility header preserves the restrictions needed for historical browser handling; the current policy header expresses restrictions on camera access and clipboard writing. When both are present, neither can be treated as a substitute for the other.

The same-origin base URL restriction is also part of the response policy. The corresponding directive is written as `base-uri 'self'`. The same-origin scope here is unrelated to frontend file paths: it is neither derived from clipboard-related code nor a byproduct of a page-local feature. Assessments should examine the page response directly.

The decision on offline assets sits alongside the response requirements, but is not a footnote to the response headers. When a page loads offline dependencies by module name, first confirm whether the name exists, then confirm whether `config/importmap.rb` provides a mapping, and finally confirm whether the mapping target resolves to a local asset. `@popperjs/core` and `vendor/javascript/@popperjs--core--esm.js` are retained as the current starting points for verification; if any of the three elements—name, mapping, or file—is missing, the offline module issue should not be recorded as resolved.

This does not exclude `clipboard.js` from frontend assets, nor does it assert that the file has no connection to any page. What is being withdrawn is the implicit attribution in the old record: this file is not the place to assess the response policy. For response issues, inspect the response directly; for offline module issues, start with the relationship between the name, mapping, and local target.

## Adjacent issues not yet separated out

In the old search results, clipboard, base, and self often appeared together, so readers may still interpret them as pointing to a single implementation location. At present, we can only confirm that these terms make the old path a useful starting point; we cannot confirm that they belong to the same runtime location. If this material is organized further, "why these search terms cluster together" and "where the page response is generated" should be treated as two separate questions.

The scope of offline assets has not been expanded to include all vendor files either. The current decision covers only local asset relationships that need to be resolved by module name. Ordinary static resources, container preparation steps, and other release files are not automatically included in this assessment just because this page exists.

Another unresolved issue still comes from the original record: whether references in the old paths still correspond to the relationships used by the current frontend. If the references have changed, the paths remain valuable as historical entry points, but can no longer serve as current navigation. This question needs to be answered at the reference sites, not inferred from response headers or local directories.

## Appendix: Old Examples

**Old example one: directory inspection.** Earlier notes would say "the offline portion is complete" after seeing that the vendor directory contained the target scripts. This example is now suitable only for illustrating a minimal asset-level check. It ignores module names and mappings and cannot serve as a complete assessment under the current decision.

**Old example two: inferring the response from functionality.** A note once suggested checking the relevant restrictions only when the page visibly used the camera or clipboard. That approach has been overturned. Page functionality provides clues at the UI and script layers; the current requirement is to use the browser's page response as the basis.

**Old example three: the script name identifies the policy location.** `vendor/javascript/clipboard.js` was once treated as the primary place to look for clipboard restrictions. This path is still retained because it leads back to the historical search context; however, the script name no longer determines where the policy belongs. When page restrictions need to be confirmed, inspect the response first, rather than only inspecting that file.

When similar symptoms arise later, there is no need to copy this page wholesale into a lengthy procedure. If the issue concerns page restrictions, start with the page response; if it concerns offline modules, start with module names, mappings, and local assets. The historical paragraphs are retained because the early combined assessment both saved time and obscured failures at different layers. The current decision is governed by the response requirements and offline module boundaries stated later on this page.

# Audit Pagination and Theme Strategy Proposal

This round of API review discusses audit-page pagination and theme modes together solely because both fall within the closeout scope of 2.3.0; that does not mean they should use the same implementation criteria.

For the audit page, compare two approaches first. One lets the page determine previous and next pagination solely from the current response contents. The change is small, but callers cannot determine the total count or whether they are on the last page. The other retains navigation and page-count information in the API response for the client to read. The initial draft leans toward the latter, provided that this information has the same meaning for successful requests and empty results.

For now, use `app/controllers/api/v1/pushes_controller.rb` as the review entry point. It helps revisit the adjacency relationship around API at the time, but it cannot be used to put page interaction, audit record generation, and response formatting in the same place.

Keep theme modes out of the pagination API. The candidates are to treat theme selection as the page's own state or to add a server-side preference that can be read back. The former avoids another API constraint; the latter makes cross-page consistency easier. There is not enough material yet to decide which one is worth bringing into this round.

Withdrawal conditions: If pagination metadata can appear only in partial results, or if the theme proposal requires changing the audit API's response shape, stop advancing the two as a combined effort. Capture the actual page behavior for one successful call and one failed call.

# Audit Pagination and Theme Strategy Proposal

The initial draft incorrectly wrote "the same review round" as "the same API closeout point." During review, retain this incorrect assumption because it explains why the theme discussion was put into the audit page's backlog at the time; but it is not suitable as a basis for subsequent changes.

What the audit page actually needs to solve is whether callers can continue paginating without guessing the total number of records. When the page receives only the current set of records, it can display the results but cannot reliably distinguish "there is no next page" from "the next page has not been fetched yet." The candidate proposal is therefore changed to: the API provides navigation information along with the current page, items per page, total record count, and total page count; the page consumes these values and does not infer boundaries from the item count.

It had not yet been decided whether the controller should assemble these values directly or whether the existing pagination layer should provide them. `app/controllers/api/v1/pushes_controller.rb` remains the reading entry point and is no longer treated as evidence of implementation ownership. If the pagination layer already has a standard response format, adding a separate format for the audit page would give callers two ways to read the response; if there is no existing format, first confirm whether empty pages, last pages, and error responses each retain the same fields.

The theme discussion has also been narrowed. The original "server-side preference" approach treated the theme as part of the audit object, at the cost of bringing a page action under the API version constraint. Another approach only requires the theme control on the admin page to work across layouts, with persistence handled separately. This trial does not write the theme value into the audit response, nor does it use whether the audit page paginates as validation of the theme proposal.

The two observations do not substitute for each other. # Audit Pagination and Theme Strategy Proposal

This proposal remains in the review entry point at 2.3.0, mainly because the earlier discussion left two easily confused concerns side by side: what the audit page uses to continue paging, and who owns theme actions in the admin UI. Later implementation and page details should not be inferred from this old proposal; this is a record of why the boundaries were drawn at the time.

## Original Starting Point

The working assumption in the first draft was that as long as the audit page received a set of records, it could infer whether more pages were available. That assumption looked convenient and also encouraged treating theme mode as another "page state issue." The counterexample was straightforward: the records in the current response are not the complete record set, and the item count does not indicate the current page's position. The first draft's wording about "handling navigation and themes through the same interface" was therefore retained as an earlier position, but was no longer adopted.

`app/controllers/api/v1/pushes_controller.rb` was included in the notes at the time so the review could start from the API entry point. It does not establish ownership of theme controls, nor is it enough to prove that all pagination information is assembled there. That distinction later mattered: the contract callers use to read page navigation and the availability of theme actions across layouts require different caller-side checks.

## Two Approaches Compared in Review

One approach lets the page decide button states from the number of results returned. Its advantage is minimal interface changes; its drawback is that empty results, the last page, and a next page that has not yet loaded all collapse into the same page-side decision. The other approach has the response specify the page position and overall range, which the page then uses to render navigation. The latter adds to the response shape but avoids making callers guess boundaries from record contents.

The review did not consider "can display Previous and Next" sufficient. Callers must be able to obtain navigation relations and page-count information from the same response; otherwise, the page will still use different inference rules in different branches. The goal here is not to give audit records new meaning, but to establish how the page reads pagination information.

There were two candidates for theme mode. One keeps the selection in the browser page and requires the same control entry point in all relevant layouts; the other makes the selection a preference that can be read back from the server. The former leaves the audit interface unchanged, but restoring the selection across pages depends on frontend state; the latter appears more unified, but would expand the maintenance scope of API and preference data. The original plan did not choose between these approaches. It only required that theme fields not be slipped in as part of the pagination changes.

## Interface Statement After Re-review

Later feedback rejected the earlier judgment that "the current record count is enough." Audit callers need stable access to navigation and counts, rather than inferring interface semantics from page behavior. The interface statement ultimately added to the review record was: The audit pagination endpoint returns Link navigation plus X-Page, X-Per-Page, X-Total, and X-Total-Pages headers with a stable page contract.

This statement defines the boundary for reading audit pagination information; it does not describe theme persistence. The old draft placed the two too close together, making it sound as though theme switching also had to go through the same response. That was the main point this proposal needed to correct. Whether theme actions are available in each admin layout still needs to be checked on the page side; the audit pagination response is not responsible for that.

## Stop Conditions During Trials

Pagination trials should start with a normal page and a page with no more records. The former confirms that the page can read navigation and counts; the latter confirms that the page no longer substitutes "this page has fewer items" for explicit boundary information. If either branch lacks the same set of response information, the frontend should not fill the gap by guessing. Revisit the pagination response design instead.

Theme trials only check whether the control entry point is available in both the home page and jobs layouts. If making the two consistent requires adding theme data to the audit response, stop this combined approach. That is not a small patch; it ties the two kinds of state together again.

The original proposal considered server-side preferences as the default direction. That remains recorded as an option that was not adopted. It was not proven wrong; there simply was not enough reason in this round to expand the interface boundary. If restoring themes across pages is genuinely needed later, compare the maintenance costs of browser-side storage and server-side preferences on their own, rather than drawing a conclusion from the audit page's pagination needs.

## Open Questions

The earlier review did not settle whether empty results should appear on the page as a normal endpoint or a separate state. This material also does not decide whether the theme selection should be restored after the browser is closed. Neither changes the requirement for stable navigation and counts in the pagination response, but both will affect how later page acceptance criteria are written.

This record explains why the earlier review split the concerns; it does not retain the final decision on theme implementation.

# Push Capability Compatibility Migration Record

Initially, compatibility checking was placed near the response for push API. The entry point is provisionally recorded as `app/controllers/api/v1/pushes_controller.rb`; this is suitable for checking the version response and the fields received by the caller, but not for splitting attachment, QR code, and parameter handling into three unrelated records.

The working assumption at the time was that callers should not infer available capabilities from the push name, page functionality, or local configuration. They should obtain the version response first, then decide whether to show the corresponding entry based on that response. This determination covers only the client's discovery phase; push creation, attachment handling, and the QR code page itself remain on their respective paths.

During the migration, retain the old caller first, then add the capability check where the version information is read. Do not fold secret parameter filtering and capability checking into the same change: the former should continue to be checked separately in the call chain that uses the parameter, while the latter should only handle consumption of the version response. If a compatibility issue appears, the new read branch can be removed first without also changing the parameter entry point.

Provisional check order:

1. Find the caller that reads the version information and record the response shape it currently depends on.
2. Add the capability check only there, and confirm that unrecognized fields do not block the existing push entry.
3. Return to the parameter caller to check secret parameter filtering, avoiding bringing request parameters into the version-response determination.
4. If the caller cannot continue working, restore the original read branch and record which consumer cannot accept the new shape.

There is not yet enough material here to explain how all clients handle missing capabilities, and there is no conclusion about where parameter filtering is implemented. The next review should fill in these two points first, rather than expanding the generic notes around the controller.

# Push Capability Compatibility Migration Record

This record has changed from a note to "add a check next to the version response" into two parallel migration tracks: one handles capability discovery, while the other continues to track secret parameter filtering. Both will be part of the same set of compatibility checks, but they have different rollback points when something fails.

## The early agreement still stands

The original agreement was that capability discovery would not replace the existing push flow. Callers would first use the existing version-reading entry point; only callers able to consume capability information would use it to adjust the UI or subsequent choices. This kept the scope of changes narrow at the time, but meant legacy callersFang Ke could continue treating capabilities as implicit conditions.

The old record included the statement, "As long as reading the version does not return an error, all push entry points can be handed over to the new branch." This is no longer a basis for the migration. An actual review found that the issue was not whether the version read returned, but whether consumers treated the capabilities in the response as optional information. The old assessment is kept here so its origin can be identified when working with historical branches.

## Keep the two tracks separate

Capability discovery concerns the version response and the consumers that read it. Its migration starts at an existing read point: first confirm that consumers can still obtain the version information they previously used, then let them use capability information to decide whether to proceed to attachment or QR code entry points. This should not also change push creation requests, nor should a client's parameter-passing behavior be changed just because it has not yet adopted capability checks.

Secret parameter filtering concerns callers that still use that parameter. Find the actual entry point first, then check the version used by that entry point and its current result. It can share a release check with capability discovery, but "the version response has been updated" is not grounds for declaring parameter filtering complete. The boundaries are:

```text
Legacy caller ──Read version information──> Existing push selection
                 │
                 └──Capability discovery branch──> Attachment/QR code entry checks

Parameter caller ──secret parameter filtering──> Its own request handling
```

The two tracks in the diagram can be checked together at release time, but must be restored separately. If capability checks fail, first remove the new branch on the read side so the caller returns to its existing choices. If parameter filtering has a problem, restore only the relevant parameter caller's old handling; do not use that as a reason to remove the compatibility work around the version response.

## Counterexamples from the review

After the review, "a response means compatibility is complete" is no longer accepted. One consumer can successfully read version information without treating the newly added capabilities as optional fields; another may only expose a problem when entering the attachment or QR code path. Checks therefore need to start at the consumption point, rather than merely looking for related names in the controller file.

`app/controllers/api/v1/pushes_controller.rb` remains the starting point for this follow-up review. Use that file by first looking at the declarations adjacent to the version response and the return shape, then going back to the callers that actually read it. Do not infer ownership of secret parameter filtering from this path; the available material only requires finding and checking callers that still use that parameter.

## Migration sequence

1. List the consumers that will read version information in this migration, and retain their pre-change read branches.
2. Confirm for each consumer that unknown or not-yet-adopted capabilities will not invalidate its existing push choices.
3. Use capability information only where attachment or QR code entry checks are actually needed; do not expand it into a master switch for push creation.
4. Identify callers using secret parameter filtering separately, and record their entry points, actual versions, and current results.
5. If capability checks cause an abnormal consumer state, first restore that consumer's original read branch; if parameter handling is abnormal, restore the corresponding parameter path. Neither restoration overrides the other.

Here, "abnormal state" means only that a caller failed to maintain its expected state after capability checks were integrated. It does not attribute the issue to the controller, response fields, or parameter filtering. The next record needs to include the affected consumer and its inputs and outputs; until then, the review results should not be generalized to mean that all callers have completed the migration.

# Push Capability Compatibility Migration Record

This page preserves part of the migration history of push version information from "callers guessing for themselves" to "callers reading capabilities." The controller entry point has always been recorded at `app/controllers/api/v1/pushes_controller.rb`. It is a place to check near the version response, and where several later discussions converged again; it is not the central entry point for attachment, QR code, or parameter handling.

When using this page now, first split the issue into two parts. Capability discovery answers whether the client can learn from the version response that a certain type of push is supported; secret parameter filtering requires going back to the callers that still use that parameter. Both can be reviewed in the same compatibility release, but a result for one must not be used to draw a conclusion about the other.

## The Earliest Recorded Migration Approach

The earliest record described only a very narrow migration approach: retain the existing version lookup and add a branch for callers that can consume additional capability information. The focus at that time was to avoid scattering feature checks across push creation points. Callers without a capability branch would continue using the existing selection logic; callers preparing to adopt the new branch would first read the version information, then decide whether to enter the relevant entry point.

At the time, "successful version lookup" was treated as a rough signal that the migration was complete. That approximation later proved too coarse. It did not distinguish among a successful lookup, the consumer accepting the response shape, and the consumer using capabilities at the actual entry point. The old approach remains documented because some older callers were connected in exactly that order; seeing it should not lead to copying it again, nor does it mean historical branches must be treated as invalid code.

The diagram from that time is also preserved below:

```text
Caller ──Version lookup──> Continue with the existing push selection
```

It did not show capability fields or discuss parameters. That was not a missing specification section, but the boundary of the migration scope before it had been expanded.

## Notes Beside the Controller

Later notes shifted attention back to the consumers of the version response, rather than merely whether a response was returned. `app/controllers/api/v1/pushes_controller.rb` can be used to confirm local declarations and adjacent relationships near the version response; starting the investigation here helps avoid guessing the source of capabilities based on page or push names.

The notes also preserve an approach that was once convenient but should no longer be used: grouping attachment support, QR code support, and parameter filtering together under "version compatibility." Doing so would make a single rollback affect three different categories of objects at once. Capability discovery is a decision on the reading side; secret parameter filtering is processing along the parameter call chain. Their only stable overlap is that, at release time, both require knowing whether the actual callers are still using the old path.

Therefore, this page has never identified the controller file as the implementation location for parameter filtering. It only provides a shared place to start checking. For parameter issues, find the callers that still use that parameter and record the entry point, actual version, and current result. Without these details, do not substitute a filename or feature name for verification.

## Failure Record After a Review

An actual review was conducted during an intermediate update. The initial intent was to treat "obtaining version information" as sufficient proof, but the conclusion retained after the review was: this only shows that a read occurred, not that the consumer is already using capability information to maintain the existing state.

The failed attempt was not a case of the controller returning no information, nor of an incorrect parameter value. The failure was in the granularity of the migration assessment: a consumer could read the response but did not treat the newly added capabilities as optional information; the problem might only surface when entering an attachment- or QR-code-related entry point. The previous practice of "merge as long as reading raises no errors" was therefore crossed out.

This review did not provide a list of all consumers, nor did it prove that every old branch needed to change. Leaving this gap is more useful than filling it with an assumed list: migration starts at specific read points, and each time a consumer is added, separately confirm that it retains its existing choices when capability information is not adopted, is missing, or is not recognized.

The recovery action described in the old version was also too general: at the time, it said "restore the old logic if a problem occurs." It is now explained separately for each affected component. If the problem occurs in capability checks, first remove the new branch on that consumer's read side so that it returns to its original push choices. If the problem occurs in secret parameter filtering, restore only the old handling for the corresponding parameter caller. Do not use a parameter problem as a reason to remove independently verified changes around the version response, and do not use a capability problem as a reason to change the parameter entry point.

## The Rejected Consolidation Plan

One option considered was to have all push entry points pass through a single shared check, then pass the result to request creation and parameter handling. It appeared to reduce the number of call sites, but it would mix two kinds of failure: failure to consume capability information would block the request path, while changes to parameter handling would lead troubleshooting back to the same master switch.

That plan was not pursued further. It is retained here because similar ideas may still appear in old discussions or localized changes. For the current migration, the version response only provides consumers with a basis for capability discovery; request parameters are still handled by their own call chains. What needs to be shared is not a piece of master-switch code, but the verification sequence within the same release.

Another old idea was that once a new caller adopted capability checks, the old read branches could be cleaned up at the same time. This no longer applies either. Restoring the old path depends on the old branches still being present, so they must be retained at least until every affected consumer can clearly identify its read entry point and current result. "Retained" here refers to the migration arrangement, not to redefining the old behavior as a current requirement.

## Notes Alongside the Review

An addendum from one review required "who reads the version response" and "who passes the secret parameter" to be written out separately. The reason was not to establish a larger list, but that the records at the time tended to treat feature names as call relationships. After the review, the wording was changed to: first locate capability checks among consumers of the version response, then locate filtering behavior among the actual users of the parameters.

Another comment was left in place: if a caller relies only on the old choices, it does not have to migrate at the same time just because capability discovery has begun elsewhere. This comment preserved the boundary for gradual migration. It does not mean that old callers will never need to be reviewed; it simply rejects presenting components that do not read the version response as though they have already adopted capability discovery.

The review also did not decide to map all capabilities to the same kind of client-side presentation. The version response is responsible for providing an entry point for discovery, while individual consumers still decide whether they need to use it to display attachment- or QR-code-related features. This keeps compatibility checks for the version response and specific user-interface behavior from being described as the same issue.

## Work Sequence for This Round of Follow-up Checks

When migrating from the old path to capability reading, follow the sequence below to avoid moving discovery logic and parameter logic together in a single change.

1. Starting at the actual point where version information is read, confirm that the caller's original selection is still present. Do not first infer capabilities backward from the push creation request.
2. Before adding capability checks at this read point, identify the old branch that should continue when capability information cannot be recognized or has not yet been adopted.
3. Connect capability checks only to attachment- or QR-code-related entry points that need them. Callers that do not use these entry points must not be changed merely because their names are similar.
4. Find other callers that still use secret parameter filtering, and verify their entry points, actual versions, and current results. Do not use the version response as a substitute for this verification.
5. If an abnormal status occurs on the read side, first restore the consumer's original selection after reading the version; if a problem occurs on the parameter path, restore the old handling for that parameter caller. Keep the issue record after the restoration; do not merge the two types of rollback into a single "compatibility failure."

The migration can be compared before and after using this simple diagram:

```text
Before migration
Caller ──read version information──> original push selection
Parameter caller ──parameter handling──> request path

After migration
Caller ──read version information──> capability check ──> original selection or relevant entry point
Parameter caller ──secret parameter filtering──> request path
```

The diagram does not connect the capability check to the parameter caller; this is intentional. The two lines appear together in the compatibility review, but they should not take over each other's handling without an explicit caller relationship.

## Correction points for the 2025 year

More recent records further tightened the old conclusion: an abnormal status occurred after capability discovery processing, and one item also remained unconfirmed. This phenomenon is left in the regression report rather than being attributed here to the controller or parameter filtering. It changes the checking threshold; it does not overturn the entire early migration direction.

PWP-204 record this status anomaly and unconfirmed item. The card is used to locate the regression record from that time; the operational requirements retained on this page remain to identify the specific consumer first and then determine its capability-reading branch. Do not treat the status changes on the card as proof that all callers have completed migration.

This also corrects the old document's wording that "the presence of capability information is enough to switch entry points." Presence, readability, and correct consumption are three different states. The current review confirms migration only when it can identify the consumer and its read branch; all other objects continue to use the old path until they have their own review result.

## 2023-06-26: Initial entry

The earliest migration ticket did not treat capability discovery as an interface contract; it described it only as a probe before a client was ready to switch entry points. The recorder copied the old branch from the version-reading location and added "check parameters separately" beside it. The value of this ticket is not in providing today's fields, but in showing that the two workstreams had no shared recovery action from the outset: restore the consumer's previous selection when discovery logic fails, and restore the actual parameter-passing caller when the parameter chain fails.

There was no consumer list at the time, and attachments and QR codes were merely two categories of entry points discussed. The on-call handoff therefore required only that the original read branch be retained and that whoever was preparing to try it be noted. This approach later seemed conservative, but it avoided expanding the ownership of navigation in one controller to the entire push system without sufficient evidence. The old ticket remains archived as it was; when citing it today, cite only this boundary.

## 2024-02: The Browser Team's Margin Review

The browser team took over a compatibility investigation once. They first used the old client to read the same version response, then used the client being prepared for migration to go through the relevant entry points. Both reads succeeded, but no verifiable observation was recorded at the time as to whether the second client actually made its selection based on capabilities. The meeting minutes briefly described the two green results as "consumers are compatible"; the margin review subsequently circled and struck out that statement, explicitly noting that green covered only the read operation.

That review also clarified a recovery signal that was easy to confuse. The client displaying its original entry point again proves only that it has returned to its previous selection; it does not prove that the version response has not changed. Conversely, the version response remaining readable does not prove that attachment or QR code entry points are already being routed according to capabilities. Subsequent migration tickets must record response-side observations and consumer-side observations separately; if either is missing, the status remains migration in progress.

## 2025-09-12: Temporary Ownership Transfer

PWP-204 was transferred to a teammate while the owner was on leave. The handoff did not redefine the requirements; it carried over only three things: the entry point beside the controller for checking back, the consumers that had not yet been confirmed, and which read branch to restore first if an anomaly occurred. The person taking over had no authority to confirm filtering results on behalf of parameter callers, so secret parameter filtering remained under PWP-221 and was not included in this capability review.

During the transfer, someone proposed marking all old consumers as covered in one go, on the grounds that they shared version reading. This proposal was not adopted. A shared entry point can only reduce lookup costs; it cannot copy observations from one consumer to another. Each item on the list still needs its own original selection, capability-reading location, and recovery signal; items that have not actually been exercised remain marked as unconfirmed.

## 2025-09-15: Regression Report Addendum

The public comments recorded an abnormal state after capability discovery processing and noted that one point remained unconfirmed. The report did not attribute the anomaly to the controller, field naming, or a specific client implementation, because only the inputs and outputs had been retained at the time, with no evidence of the intermediate selection. On that basis, the review changed the merge requirement from "the request succeeds" to "we can identify the branch in which the consumer makes its selection".

This addendum also defined the stopping point for the report: after reproducing the anomaly, first save that consumer's read results and entry-point state before and after the change, then restore its own old branch. Do not modify parameter callers along the way just to make the report look complete, and do not overwrite the original anomaly with the green status after restoration. If it cannot be reproduced next time, add an observation and retain the previous one; do not rewrite history as though it never happened.

## 2025-09-16: Division of responsibilities after entering re-review

Once the card moved to in progress, the API side was responsible for confirming what was actually visible around the version response, the client side was responsible for confirming how the read point used it, and the on-call team member maintained only the restoration record. The materials from all three parties needed to point to the same consumer, but did not have to be written on the same page. This preserved an important distinction: the API side could confirm the response shape, only the client side could confirm the entry-point selection, and the on-call side could only confirm whether restoration was complete.

The review excerpt was brief:

> First make clear which consumer, which read, and which restoration signal; leave all other callers unknown.

This excerpt later became the checking order used throughout the rest of this page. It did not add any new capabilities or make judgments about unconfirmed subjects; it only prevented the same green record from being reused across multiple consumers. When the documentation was finalized on 2025-09-29, the parameter callers that still had not been found remained in an adjacent issue, rather than being closed out by the capability discovery results.

## 2025-09-29: Handoff table before archiving

The final cleanup before archiving did not rewrite earlier conclusions; instead, it put each piece of material back into the column for its own area of responsibility. The column for the API side recorded only where to verify the version response and the results visible on that occasion; the consumer column recorded the actual read point, the original selection, and observations after integration; the on-call column recorded the restoration signal and when restoration occurred. A separate row was retained for secret parameter filtering, containing only the adjacent item pending investigation, without listing a caller that had not yet been found as the owner on the API side.

The handoff table still retains two incomplete statuses. The first is "response readable, consumption unverified," meaning the caller received the version information, but the records are insufficient to prove that it changed its entry point based on the capability. The second is "consumer recovered, exception unattributed," meaning the old choice is available again, but the original exception may still have come from reading, selection, or some other local state. Neither status can be marked complete, and there is no need to force a single root cause for the sake of archiving.

This cleanup uses item-by-item closure rather than closing the entire batch. A consumer is removed from the migration only when its original read path, capability-check location, actual observations, and recovery method all line up. Another consumer retains its own status even if it shares the same controller entry point. This allows new and old clients to be at different migration stages, and when a problem occurs, only the affected item can be rolled back.

If only verbal confirmation is obtained during the handoff, record the confirmer and the evidence still to be supplied in the table; do not rewrite a verbal conclusion as an observed result. When follow-up material arrives, append it under the corresponding consumer row and preserve its timing relationship showing that it came after the exception or recovery. This makes it possible to determine whether the new evidence explains the earlier incident or merely describes the state after recovery. If the confirmer later cannot reverify it, leave the original row as unverified rather than converting it into team consensus; the next person taking over should observe it again from the same read point.

The check statement left by the archivist is: locate by consumer first, assess by evidence next, and hand off based on the recovery signal last. Each handoff closes only one item and preserves the time and original record. It coexists with the old appendix earlier on this page so that the person taking over can see how the rules were corrected, rather than seeing only the cleaned-up answer. If a parameter caller is found later, add its version and date and state whether it actually has a call relationship with the current consumer; do not go back and add to the old paragraph an attribution that makes it appear to have been known at the time.
## Current Version Response Convention

After the layers of old records, reviews, and corrections described above, the current compatibility requirement is limited to the version capability response: The API version capability response names file_attachments and qr_code_pushes so clients can discover attachment and QR-code push support.

The migration significance of this convention is narrow. Clients read these two capability names from the version response and use them to determine whether to recognize attachment-push and QR-code-push support; it does not require clients to rewrite all push behavior as capability checks, nor does it fold request-parameter handling into the same branch. For legacy callers that have not yet been integrated, retain the existing selection and migrate them only after the caller has an independent verification at the read end.

During execution, record separately where the field appears and whether the consumer uses it. Verify the former near the version response and the latter at the specific read point. Looking only at the controller is insufficient to prove that the consumer has migrated; looking only at the consumer name is also insufficient to confirm that it reads the current response. Only when both sides line up should the consumer be switched from the old path to capability checking.

Restoring the old path should also follow this boundary. If a consumer ends up in an abnormal state after capability detection is integrated, roll back that consumer's read-side changes and restore its original push selection; do not remove the capability names from the version response, and do not use this to conclude that other consumers must roll back. If the issue found is secret parameter filtering, restore only the previous handling for the relevant parameter caller, then continue to retain the verification record for capability discovery.

## Remaining adjacent issue not yet split out

secret parameter filtering remains an independent item requiring investigation. A caller that is still using this parameter must be found, and its actual version, entry point, and current result must be verified. The current material has not pinpointed this caller in a controller file, nor explained whether it shares a consumer with the attachment or QR-code entry points; therefore, it cannot be written as an incidental conclusion of the capability-response change.

The next update should first clearly document the actual entry point of this caller, and then determine whether it needs to be handled in the same batch as capability discovery. If the update only says "someone is still using the parameter", this page still cannot use that to change the current migration order.

## Retained legacy appendices

### Legacy Appendix A: Use successful version retrieval as the completion criterion

> If reading the version information produces no errors, the caller can be considered compatible with the new push capability.

Deprecated. It comes from an earlier migration record with a smaller scope and is retained only to explain why the old branch had no capability check.
