# Payload Accessibility Pilot Plan

2.3.0 Before closeout, payload accessibility state was treated as an open gap in the API review: the issue was not whether to add another description to the payload, but whether callers could distinguish the current visibility handling from the same entry point. Existing records place the verification entry at `app/controllers/pushes_controller.rb`; this is only a convenient place to start checking and should not be taken to mean that state ownership has been determined.

The working assumption at the time was that organizing the state at the controller response boundary would make compatibility impact easier to see than changing page controls first. There is one clear counterexample: if the same payload gets different masking or disclosure results on different user paths, a single state from the API layer will hide the difference. The draft did not have such a counterexample, so it did not record "a single state is sufficient" as a decision.

The proposed first step is a narrow pilot:

- Select existing payload paths that go through pushes controller, and record the visibility signals already present in the response instead of creating another set of presentation fields;
- Compare the results before and after the payload moves from a restricted state to a readable state, confirming whether callers actually need a stable state rather than only the current page's presentation;
- Record the controller return value, page transition, and test case separately. Matching results for the first two does not mean the third can also be reused.

This order favors the API side; the trade-off is that accessibility details in the page implementation will temporarily remain outside the verification scope. Someone previously suggested locking down the state name directly because it would make later regression testing easier; that was not adopted here. Once a name enters the API, existing clients will treat it as a long-term commitment, while there is still no conclusion on whether the state is consistent across paths.

The withdrawal criteria should also be simple: if the pilot can only demonstrate the presentation effect of one page, or if the state requires page-private conditions to be interpretable, stop promoting it to an API state and retain the page-side handling. If the controller can provide an independent, verifiable state and the semantics of the two phases do not overlap, then discuss whether to lock down a public name.

This draft retains the judgment that "the controller entry comes first," so the reason the presentation layer was not modified directly at the time can be reviewed later. It has not completed the state enumeration or confirmed which layer should own it. Subsequent verification still starts at `app/controllers/pushes_controller.rb`; what needs to be added are specific user paths that could disprove the assumption.

# Recipient Validation Migration Check

This migration addresses where compatibility checks should be anchored. Early records gathered clues by issue name, call name, and scattered keywords, which made searching quick, but also put the API entry point, recipient collections, notification calls, and background processing into the same note. The most likely mistake during handoff is to turn a name match into "this is responsible for validation," then fill in relationships that have not actually been inspected based on that judgment.

The old records are still retained, but their purpose has changed: they take people back to the original search scope; the current review starts from `app/controllers/api/v1/pushes_controller.rb` and separates locations already inspected from directions not yet explored. What is being migrated is the checking method, not ownership of all recipient-related objects to the controller.

## Do Not Turn the Old Records into Conclusions Yet

If the old notes contain only "recipient validation" or a notification call name, keep that text unchanged at the beginning of this round's record. It explains why the investigation went toward API, and can restore the original entry point if the new path is interrupted. Do not first merge similar terms into a single "recipient processing flow."

The following types of matches look adjacent in the old records, but each should retain its own source:

- `recipient` may appear next to request or response text;
- `recipients` may just be a name near a collection, parameter, or call;
- notification indicates a notification context, but cannot by itself prove that a notification has been created;
- `validated` is a historical search term, and cannot by itself determine the validation location;
- `before` and job can only suggest a sequencing direction, not replace a call relationship.

This does not require searching every term again each time. It is enough for the old notes to identify the original match locations. New records should add only file locations actually opened in this round, adjacent references, or an explicit "not yet explored." A term appearing again in different locations does not need to be forcibly merged either; first check whether it connects to the same object.

## Starting Point After Migration

After opening the controller file, start with a narrowly scoped two-column split. Keep candidates from the old search on the left, and write only the direct locations already inspected in the current file on the right. If the current location is a call site, record it as a call site; if it is only text with the same name, label it accordingly. Do not fill in return results, rejection actions, or value transformations just to make the record complete.

```text
Old notes                      Current review
Issue name / call name         app/controllers/api/v1/pushes_controller.rb
        |                                  |
        +-- recipient, recipients          +-- Locations actually inspected in the current file
        +-- notification, validated        +-- Adjacent references available for further inspection
        +-- before, job                    +-- Directions not yet explored in this round

Restore the old path: return to the original match location      Continue the new path: explore from the recorded references
```

The two sides of the diagram are not two implementation branches. The left side is how the old material locates things, and the right side is how this compatibility check records them. If no corresponding location can be found for the old entry point, write "no corresponding location," rather than forcing it onto a line in the controller. Names seen in the controller do not automatically substantiate the old records either; the two sides may be connected in the notes only after they connect at the same actual location or reference.

## Sequence for One Round of Checking

First copy the issue names and call names from the old records, retaining the original adjacent terms. Then inspect the controller file and divide what you see this time into three categories: direct objects within the current file, call sites leading out of the current file, and candidate directions that still exist only in the old notes. This sequence is more reliable than first discussing "where validation happens," because it avoids mistaking a file entry point for ownership of behavior.

Next, continue only along adjacent references already seen. If this round reveals a notification direction, record "need to inspect how this call obtains recipients," rather than "the notification uses a certain kind of recipient value." If this round reveals a background processing direction, record "there is a direction yet to be explored," rather than "rejection occurs in the background." For compatibility checks, stopping at this step is normal; the record must let later readers distinguish what came from this round's inspection from questions left by the old search.

When encountering objects with the same name, first ask two local questions: does it appear at the point of entry into API, or at a call leading out of the current file? Is there an actual reference connecting it to another candidate? Only when the second question has a definite answer should recipients, notifications, or job be written in the same observation. Identical names, adjacent paragraphs, or appearances in the same set of search results are not enough.

### Failing Input

The question left by the initial draft, "at which layer is failing input rejected," remains unresolved. When handling it, do not tuck it under the record of recipient names. Create a separate entry to record the failure behavior already observed and any references that can be connected to it; if no rejection action was seen in this round, retain only the question itself. The controller is the API entry point, which does not mean it necessarily owns the rejection decision.

This unresolved item has practical value: it prevents later readers from conflating "the request passes through the controller" with "the controller rejects the request." If subsequent references connect the rejection location back to the current file, add the specific location under this entry; if they connect elsewhere, retain that separation as well. The vague use of "validation" in the old notes does not need to be deleted, but it no longer serves as evidence for the rejection layer.

### Recipient Values for Notifications

Record the notification direction separately as well. What needs to be checked is whether notification-related calls receive the original recipients or processed values, not merely whether the word notification can be found. If only a notification name is seen, record "call exists or remains to be explored"; if only a collection name is seen, record "value form unconfirmed." The two must be connected by an actual call relationship before they can be written as a single observation in the compatibility record.

This distinction also applies to `recipient` and `recipients`. The singular/plural difference may simply reflect naming at different locations, and cannot be used to infer where values are collected, processed, or passed. If the value form of a reference is confirmed later, add the observation under the corresponding call entry, rather than going back and rewriting every section of the old search notes.

## Minimal Record Format

A review does not need to become a complete walkthrough. The following five items are enough to keep the old entry points alongside the current inspection results:

| Item | How to record it |
| --- | --- |
| Old location information | Issue name, call name, and original match location |
| Current file | Direct objects or call sites already inspected |
| Reference direction | Adjacent references already opened, or directions not yet explored |
| Failing input | Observed behavior; leave unresolved if there is no rejection location |
| Notification recipients | Confirmed value form; otherwise write unconfirmed |

The table is not a requirement to fill in every field. A round can end after handling only the old location information and the current file; do not guess the order of notifications or job just to complete the table. Conversely, if actual inspection has ruled out an old candidate, put that result back beside the original candidate as well. This keeps the same name from being treated as a new clue next time.

## How to Restore the Old Path

When the current file does not connect to an old match, or adjacent references have not yet been explored, restoration is simple: return to the issue names and call names in the old records, start again from the original match locations, and attach new findings to the corresponding candidates. Do not interpret restoration as reverting code changes; what is being restored here is the entry point for verification.

If later inspection finds that a direction is unrelated to `app/controllers/api/v1/pushes_controller.rb`, retain that separation as well. It is more useful than a vague "possibly elsewhere," because the next review can skip a direction already inspected. PWP-214 can be used to return to the related context for this check; adjacent material on audit event provenance is at DOC-26, and should still be recorded by its respective objects, without using either side's conclusions to fill in the other.

What can currently be confirmed is that the review should start in the controller file, and that old search results must be stored separately from actual references. The rejection layer for failing input, the recipient values used by notification calls, and whether the candidate terms belong to the same validation step remain to be determined by references explored later.

The judgment at the time was: after seeing a maintenance note, it can usually be handled as temporary congestion in the release queue—preserve the state and wait for the next run. As long as the first failure is still visible, do not restart, refresh permissions, or regenerate the input.

The old record instructs you to look directly in `docs/adj-public/runbooks/public-release-automation-failed-run-on-call-page.md` for the items to inspect. That entry point can still be used for navigation, but it does not guarantee that you can recover the original failure from a given run. If all you can see are maintenance notes, screenshots, or old successful samples, the evidence is already incomplete. Explicitly write "original failure not obtained" in the record, then stop writing subsequent speculation as fact.

## The old waiting rule

Early on-call practice was as follows: if maintenance notes were visible and the release had not yet shown any clear anomaly, wait for the next queue run. When the page turned green again, the default was to classify the issue as temporary congestion. This rule was once treated as the default recovery path.

It is retained not because it is reliable, but because this is what the old handoff records actually said. It misses two cases: a failure before the workflow enters release; or a release that appears to have recovered while the artifact version and rollback action have not returned to a consistent state. Do not delete or alter the "wait" conclusion in old handoffs; start a separate line in the new record stating whether the conditions for waiting were present in that run.

## Check the run state

First confirm whether this run is visible at the entry point corresponding to `.github/workflows`.

- If the run is not visible, or the entry point only leads to an old link: stop. Record the old link and the state you can currently see; do not substitute the most recent successful run.
- If the run is visible but has not entered release: compare only the first point of difference between one normal sample and this sample. You can compare the workflow entry point, queue position, or artifact version; choose only one at a time.
- If the run has entered release: preserve the current artifact version, then check whether it has entered the rollback window. If there is a rollback window, stop advancing; do not roll back and rerun at the same time.
- If release has turned green again: you still need to check whether the handoff record includes an exit action. Green only shows that the current stage is visible, not that the entire run has been explained.

There is no requirement here to identify the root cause during the shift. The location of the first failure is more useful than assigning a cause too early. If someone wants to verify by rerunning, first confirm that the original input, current version, and first result have all been saved; otherwise, rerunning will only create another run.

## Counterexamples found later

While handling PWPA-001, only screenshots remained in the attachments, and the original failure was not obtained, so the card was blocked. This counterexample refuted the habitual assumption that "screenshots are enough to keep troubleshooting": screenshots can preserve the visible state, but cannot prove where the failure occurred. With the same kind of evidence, stop pending retrieval of the original failure, rather than linking the results in the screenshots to the queue, release, or artifact version.

PWPA-007 exposed another issue: release-related state and exit actions may be inconsistent. The old page treated partial recovery as a signal to proceed, which does not hold in this counterexample. The on-call record needs to state "whether the current stage has recovered" and "whether the exit action is confirmed" separately; if only one of the two is available, remain paused and do not treat the rollback window as over.

PWPA-012 recorded entry-point differences after a cold start. This does not prove the source of any failure, but it changed the actions before a rerun: first clear your own cache, then use the same entry point to confirm whether the difference is still there. Shared caches are outside the first round of actions on this page, because touching them would change more of the state under investigation and affect runs other people are looking at.

## Obsolete instructions still retained

> Once the queue has recovered, proceed directly with the release; if differences appear again afterward, go back and check the artifact version.

This is the exact wording from the old page and no longer applies. It ties "queue recovery" to "the release can proceed" and allows progress before the version state has been confirmed. Do not follow it, but do not delete it from historical versions, because the handoff notes for old runs depend on this path to make sense.

Another old habit was to deal with the rollback entry point first, then revisit the failure location. It applied when rollback was treated as the only visible control point; now it can only be used after release status has been confirmed. If the failure is still at the workflow entry point, starting with rollback will neither recover the original failure nor narrow the scope of the assessment.

## Handoff contents

Do not write a handoff consisting only of "recovered." Record the entry point used at the time, the location of the first failure or gap, whether you obtained the original failure or a screenshot, whether the current artifact version has been preserved, and whether the run has entered the rollback window. If there was a rerun, specify whether you only cleared your own cache beforehand, or whether other changes had already been made to the state under investigation.

The person taking over should read these items first, then decide whether to continue comparing normal samples, wait for the next run, or stop at the rollback window. If the exit action cannot be confirmed, remain stopped. PWPA-001, PWPA-007, and PWPA-012 can provide pointers on missing screenshots, inconsistent rollback state, and cold-start entry-point differences, respectively; they are not substitute evidence for the same run.

This page has not been updated to the new release process. It retains the old waiting rule and rollback sequence so that readers of old handoffs can understand why things were handled that way at the time. New failure records should start with the first visible difference, not with the default assessment on this page.

# Release Automation Cache Trade-offs

For this round of release automation, we are not rebuilding the environment; we are preserving the cache and working state for the current revision. The rationale is not that the cache is guaranteed to be reusable, but that rebuilding would erase the state still available for comparison before exit; at the time, we needed to inspect the final output before deciding whether switching environments was worthwhile.

We decided to keep maintenance notes and audit records separate. The former contains only the conditions under which the cache can continue to be used; the latter records exit actions and their results. The two sections must not be merged: a given failure can have the same outward symptoms but different exit points, and later investigations need to know where it stopped at the time.

Before releasing the current revision, preserve the exit code, public · Release Automation, and the final log segment; keep these materials with the working state, not as a substitute for a rebuild. If the cache can no longer be used, first assess the exit action based on the saved final output, then remove the cache.

The objection is that maintaining a separate audit record adds an extra pass to organize the records, and the old entry point could still be mistaken for the active path. We accept that cost here; putting everything back into the maintenance note would mix exit results with cache conditions. The tentative rollback plan is to restore only the old entry point; we still haven't established which callers are using theme mode.

# Dependency Boundary Dual-State Anomaly Review

The same object in the dependency-boundary audit showed different current revisions at two points in time. The object itself is linked to dependency sources derived from lock and license, as well as the adoption scope and exit responsibility; each of these already has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit conditions. The anomaly first appeared as a discrepancy between the audit trail and the old record, rather than as a missing dependency source.

## Observed State

The state in the old record remained readable, but the audit trail pointed the same object to a different current revision. Neither was marked as historical, so a reader could not determine from "current" alone which record to use when interpreting the adoption scope, nor confirm from that whether exit responsibility had changed. This discrepancy would send subsequent checks to two different record views.

At the time, the two states were not combined into a single explanation. The original record, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause were kept separately so that a later update to the entry point would not overwrite the state seen earlier. The incident materials are retained in `docs/adj-app/incidents/app-dependency-boundary-audit-two-states-for-one-object.md`.

## Timeline

- When the audit trail was first checked, it differed from the old record; at that point, the only confirmed fact was that the same object had two current states.
- The version observed at the time was then pinned; the original record was not replaced with the content later shown by the entry point.
- Further retries were stopped. Re-reading the entry point would not establish which of the two current revisions should serve as the basis for the adoption scope; instead, it could cause the state on the recovery page to be mistaken for a new result.
- During review, the current entry point was still the only confirmed point. No cause assessment was recorded for branches that were not reproduced; they remain among the unconfirmed items.

## Impact and Recovery

The impact centered on dependency-boundary interpretation and handoff: when checking the sources derived from lock and license, the current entry alone was insufficient to determine the adoption scope; when handling exit responsibility, neither state could be treated as a correction of the other. Recovery did not backfill a single unified revision; it preserved the records from both points in time and kept the state visible then on the recovery page.

The investigation did not establish when the revision discrepancy began, nor whether it corresponded to an actual change in the lock or license records. The state on the recovery page can be used for retrospective review; the cause remains to be established separately. Until then, both current states should be treated as the original observations left by this anomaly.

The meaning at the time was narrow: with all three sections present, the maintainers could continue preparing for the exit. This did not establish dependency provenance, the scope of adoption, or the queue state after removal. The old version treated `header contract` as a signal before cleanup; this paragraph remains as an index for reading the old records.

Later, when materials from both sides were compared, records for the same object were found to disagree. The approach in PWPB-008 was not to pick whichever page "looked newer," but to put the materials' generation times side by side and stop merging beyond the first divergence. This approach was retained because exit windows commonly leave old pages in place, rather than yield a new conclusion.

## Opening This Window

1. [ ] Start from `docs/adj-app/release/app-supply-boundary-exit-window-checklist.md` and save the checklist version, original input, and first result segment shown when you open it. This path is a maintenance entry point; it does not mean that all materials with the same name belong to this window.
2. [ ] Review lock, license, and the resulting dependency provenance separately. They may appear in the same check, but one being normal does not establish anything about the other two.
3. [ ] Record the scope of adoption and exit responsibilities alongside the materials from the same round. If the scope is unclear, record only the facts for the window; do not treat either continued or discontinued use of the dependency as established.
4. [ ] Keep one sample of a successful path and one of a rejection path. Do not compare samples directly if they come from different inputs or checklist states, or if they have undergone manual cleanup in between.

The old version required: "Do not clean up after seeing `header contract`." This now reads: do not clean up until the exit action, the last visible result, and the actual object for adj-app have been matched up. `header contract` is only a field in the old checklist, not evidence that the exit is complete. The same applies to `fixture boundary`; if it is not visible, stop there and record what is missing. Do not fill the gap with a similarly named fixture.

## Exit Actions

1. [ ] Trace back from the exit action to the actual adj-app. The reminder in PWPB-009 still applies: do not guess the actual object from the filename, page color, or directory location.
2. [ ] Before releasing the current revision, save the exit code, the identifier for app · Dependency Boundary Audit, and the final log segment. PWPB-014 restored this item to the window-closing sequence; do not release yet unless all three are present.
3. [ ] Check whether the temporary bypass has been removed. If new input is still arriving after its removal, or if you cannot determine whether the bypass is still in place, stop closing the window. Do not mark the window complete first and investigate afterward.
4. [ ] Compare the materials saved before the exit with the last visible result. If the result still shows an old value, follow PWPB-003 and retain the page where the old value was first seen and the time it was seen. It may come from an old cache or an old task; this checklist does not decide between the two.

If exit actions and results cannot be matched one to one, prioritize preserving the discrepancy itself. In particular, when the page already shows new content but the final log segment still belongs to an old task, do not stitch the two pieces of material together into a successful exit just to get a tidy record. The window stops here, and further assessment passes to the maintainers of the actual object.

## Missing Parameters

PWPB-013 noted that command parameters were missing from the original checklist. This gap has not been filled with "default parameters": parameters recovered later, results from reruns with new parameters, and commands copied from elsewhere must each be saved on separate lines from the original window materials. The old records can help locate what was examined at the time, but cannot prove that a new command reproduced the same result.

For that reason, the early statement that "the checklist version and source can be traced back" is also retained only as an old requirement. At a minimum, it must now be possible to see the sequence linking the checklist entry point, input, exit action, and last visible result. If any of these is not on hand, do not record the window as closed.

## Stopping and Handoff

Stop immediately in any of the following cases:

- The two sets of records reach their first divergence in timing or generated materials;
- The original input has been replaced, and the content used for this window can no longer be identified;
- Any of the exit code, current revision, or final log segment is missing;
- New input continues to arrive after removal of the temporary bypass;
- A rerun with unrecorded parameters is needed to explain the existing results.

After stopping, retain the materials already seen and the reason the work is incomplete. Do not add a release conclusion after the fact. Release sign-off, whether the dependency can continue to be used, and whether responsibility transfers after the exit still require separate confirmation from the respective owners.

The recovery actions in this checklist have not yet been run successfully in a shared environment. If the removal action prevents the original check from continuing, the only option is to return to the state saved before the exit; this page does not decide whether to proceed with the release.

# Quality Signal Dashboard State Anomaly Postmortem

After a test failure sample was assigned to a regression tier, the same object in the Quality Signal Dashboard showed two different states at the current entry point. The initial comparison only showed that the header contract did not match the old record; there wasn't enough evidence at the time to determine whether the object itself had changed or the entry point for the record had changed versions.

The incident state was first preserved in `docs/adj-db/incidents/db-quality-signal-board-two-states-for-one-object.md`. Further retries were stopped because each rerun would only produce a new green or red result, without answering why the old record still pointed to a different current revision.

The recovery we can confirm is that the fixture boundary can pass again. This result only shows that the boundary has recovered, not that the cause of the instability signal has been established. The original view was that header contract drift caused the state divergence, and the regression tier should use the current entry point as the source of truth. That assessment remains in place for now, and subsequent scheduling is also based on it.

```text
Failure sample -> Regression tier -> Current entry point
                    |-> Current revision in the old record
```

The impact did not extend beyond the Quality Signal Dashboard. The original failure window, object name, and entry point version will be left unchanged; the recovery results will be appended to the original record.

Missing timestamp: ____

We still need to check when each of the two current revisions was written to the entry point. If the on-duty record can't be found, this must remain undetermined; we can't infer it from the post-recovery fixture results.

versions.body:
# Postmortem of the Quality Signal Console State Anomaly

This page has never been removed from the knowledge base, not because its conclusions are reliable, but because the original records left when the two states appeared side by side still get dug up. It records the failure samples, regression tiering, and unstable signal attribution that developed around test in the Quality Signal Console. That round had its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria; the entry point has since changed several times, but the old page still retains the wording from that time.

The phrase "the same object" in the title is the easiest part to misread. What happened at the time was not two different objects overwriting each other, but the current entry point returning different current revision values at two points in time. The old record and the recovery page therefore looked as though they were describing one object simultaneously. The people who first organized the records treated this juxtaposition as a state synchronization failure, while those who came later treated it as the regression layer placing failure samples in the wrong tier. Neither explanation had the benefit of the full time window at the time.

The original incident account is retained here: what was first observed was a mismatch between header contract and the old record; fixture boundary then recovered; there was no answer as to why the unstable signals changed. This account was later used to explain the schedule, but it did not prove that header contract was the cause. The page is still retained because deleting it would also erase the rationale at the time for stopping further retries.

## What was observed, in order

The initial input came from test failure samples. When the samples were placed into regression tiers, the object state shown by the current entry point differed from the state in the original record. No one merged the two records first, because both said "current", and each "current" pointed to a different revision.

The first comparison only picked up differences in header contract. The records at the time described this as a deviation from the baseline and assumed that continuing to retry through the current entry point would reduce the inconsistency to a brief fluctuation. The retries did not provide that answer. Each round of output could only show the result of fixture boundary at that moment; it could not indicate when the old record became invalid, nor explain why the attribution of unstable signals changed along with it.

The work therefore stopped at the original entry point:

`docs/adj-db/incidents/db-quality-signal-board-two-states-for-one-object.md`

The original record was not overwritten, and the recovery page was not merged back into the failure window. Keeping them separate was practical at the time: at least it distinguished "a particular boundary has recovered" from "why two states could remain in the records simultaneously". But it also left an impression that was repeatedly misused later: it seemed that once fixture boundary passed, the entry-point discrepancy had already been addressed.

```text
Failure samples
   |
   v
Regression tiering ----> Current entry point ----> Current revision A
   |                              |
   |                              +-- Current revision B in the old record
   v
Unstable signal attribution
```

The two revision lines in the diagram merely reflect the interpretation at the time, not a verified causal diagram. The old postmortem called the divergence of the two lines in the diagram "state not synchronized"; that wording is retained here to help explain why reruns were stopped at the time. It should not be taken as an assessment of subsequent entry points.

## Original assessment and its impact

The previous assessment was "the header contract differs from the old record, so the object's state was only partially updated". It sounded as though it could explain the two states: one looked like the old record, and the other like the new entry point. Regression tiering was therefore instructed to use the results from the current entry point as the reference for now, while retaining the old record as an item pending cleanup. Scheduling was also based on this assumption: first observe whether the test samples returned to a stable tier, then decide whether to remove the old page.

This assessment had an obvious gap: it did not record when each of the two current revision values was written, nor did it leave a complete record linking the failing sample to either revision. The page contained only three sections: "first seen", "later recovered", and "cause unknown". Reading them as a complete timeline is incorrect.

At the time, this gap was not treated as a blocker. The reason was simple: the fixture boundary could already recover, the cost of continued retries was increasing, and there were no new failing samples that could narrow down the issue. As a result, "recovery" was prioritized in the schedule, while "attribution" was left for later. This order was not itself the problem; the problem was that the old page was subsequently treated as documentation of completed attribution.

During the failure window, regression tiering did not receive a single stable state. It first received failing samples, then later saw recovery results. Both were retained to prevent the green results from masking the original failure. The old version called this "two states of the same object". From a recordkeeping perspective, this description was too broad: it did not make clear whether the entry point, the sample, the record, or the tier state was changing.

The old handling instructions, which are still retained, read as follows:

- Use the revision shown at the current entry point as the short-term comparison point;
- Attach the old record to the failing sample, without deleting it immediately;
- Stop continuous retries after the fixture boundary recovers;
- Leave the cause of the unstable signal among the unconfirmed items;
- Wait for the current shift's log to be completed before deciding whether to merge the pages.

This wording was once considered sufficient because it avoided constructing a complete story without timestamps. It did indeed preserve the original failing sample. However, it did not prevent another problem: later readers took just the phrase "the fixture boundary recovered" to mean that the old record and the current entry point were already aligned.

## Recovery Is Not Attribution

After the recovery page appeared, the fixture boundary on the Quality Signal Console could pass again. This was recorded as the result of the recovery action, not as confirmation of the root cause. The original record did not connect all the inputs before and after recovery, nor did it attribute the changes in the unstable signal to any single modification.

In hindsight, what was most worth retaining was not "it has passed", but the deliberate separation at the time between recovery timing and root-cause timing. Recovery answered only one local question: whether that fixture boundary could still work. It did not answer why the current entry point returned different revision values on two reads, much less why regression tiering presented this as two states of the same object.

The old version includes the statement "the state divergence was caused by header contract drift". This statement has no chain of evidence and cannot serve as the basis for current handling. It was not removed from the page, because it explains why the early scheduling favored retries and baseline comparisons. Recasting this statement as a definitive technical conclusion would instead erase the blind spots that existed at the time.

There is another source of confusion: the recovery page was appended later, and the original failure window was not replaced. When the two pages are shown side by side, readers may assume that they must share the same current revision. In fact, the retained material is only sufficient to confirm that the entry point returned different current revision values at two points in time; it does not establish which page represents the final state.

The earlier procedure required "wait for green before clearing the old records". This instruction is retained on this page as a historical procedure and is not recommended for determining the current exit criteria. A green result can show that a test run did not reproduce the same boundary behavior, but it cannot replace the missing timing records. This is precisely why the original record, the recovery page, and the unconfirmed cause have continued to coexist.

## Why retries stopped

Repeated retries were reasonable at first. The failing sample came from test, and regression tiering also required knowing whether it was stable; if the next round still failed, at least the issue could be kept within the same observation context. But what was actually observed was that, after the fixture boundary recovered, retries no longer added information that could explain the revision divergence.

So the team stopped retrying during the incident. This stopping point was described very briefly in the old record and was later often read as "the problem was resolved". The more accurate historical meaning is: with the available inputs, further runs could not explain the entry-point version differences or identify the cause of the unstable signal. Retries were stopped to preserve the failure window, not to declare that the object now had only one state.

The original schedule conflated the following three things: whether the regression sample had recovered, whether the current entry points were consistent, and whether attribution was complete. They arose one after another during the incident, but did not have to be completed at the same time. The old postmortem did not clearly separate them, which led to the mistaken reading that "the dual-state issue had already been resolved".

At the time, the operational sequence was:

```text
Observed a failing sample
  -> Recorded regression tiering
  -> Compared the current entry point with the old record
  -> fixture boundary recovered
  -> Stopped retrying
  -> Left the cause blank
```

This operational sequence does not prove that the header contract was the cause, nor does it prove that the two revision values resulted from a single synchronization failure. It only shows that the team chose, during the incident, not to let new reruns overwrite the old sample. Filling in the blank in the last step with any definite cause would go beyond the original record.

## Gaps in the record noted later

PWPC-010 relates to the work of preserving the recovery results alongside the original incident evidence. The card's description explicitly required appending the recovery results to "db · Quality Signal Board The same object appears in two states", without overwriting the original failure window or the object. This action continued the choice made at the time of the incident: recovery material could be added, but the failure scene could not be rewritten to look like the recovered state.

In the supplementary note for 2026-02-19, the execution record was flagged as belonging to the previous version; the current result had no source attached. This reminder did not provide a new root cause, nor did it fill in the revision timing gap. It only further showed that the existence of recovery results could not automatically give the old entry point traceable context.

This addendum does not conflict with the old postmortem. The old postmortem already separated recovery from the cause, but at the time it did not explicitly state what impact "the current result has no source attached" would have. Readers who later see only the current result will not be able to tell which test run, record, or entry-point read it came from. It therefore looks like a standalone state, which in turn reinforces the appearance of "dual states".

PWPC-011 addresses the window with no records. The card requires checking with the person on duty to verify the gap for the current revision; if there is no record, it must explicitly state that no determination can be made. That time point has not been fabricated here. The blank entries left on the old page still stand: the material does not answer what happened between the two revisions.

The risk check for 2026-03-02 also exposed a maintenance issue: the replacement address for the person whose on-duty assignment had expired had not been entered. The next day's addendum further stated that this person was no longer shown as the long-term owner, and the replacement address was still blank. This issue affects subsequent attempts to locate the entry point, which does not mean it explains the cause of the incident. It only makes it harder to complete records that were already missing time points.

The old postmortem initially treated "wait for the on-duty records to be completed" as a follow-up action. Looking back now, this action did not result in an actual alternative entry point. Thus, the "waiting for further checks" note retained on the page is not completed recovery work, but a lingering issue that no longer has a clear handoff point.

## The Incorrect Attribution That Was Retained

This section is the core of the old page, and also the part that requires the most caution when referring to it in day-to-day work.

The initial attribution focused on header contract. The reasoning was that it was the first difference observed, and it seemed capable of explaining the difference between the old records and the current entry point as an unfinished update. This explanation had not been fully verified, but it fit the troubleshooting approach at the time: identify the first visible change, then check whether fixture could return to baseline.

fixture boundary was later restored, which made this explanation look even more like the answer. In fact, recovery occurred only at a single boundary. There is no material showing that changes to header contract corresponded one-to-one with the divergence between the two current revisions, nor any material showing that the regression layers produced an incorrect state as a result. The old postmortem did not get that far.

However, the lack of subsequent material is not a reason to replace the old assessment with another definitive explanation. The facts currently preserved remain very limited:

- test had produced failing samples;
- the failing samples had entered the regression layers;
- the current entry point for the same object returned different current revisions at two points in time;
- the original record, the recovery page, and the unconfirmed cause were retained separately;
- fixture boundary had been restored;
- the cause of the unstable signal was not confirmed.

These facts are insufficient to support "synchronization failure", "entry-point switching error" or "the regression layer wrote the wrong state" as a definitive conclusion. Yet the old write-up leaned toward the first explanation in its narrative, so it has been retained as an outdated postmortem that can easily mislead, rather than as the current explanation.

At the time, a simpler interpretation also emerged: the two states were merely differences in how the same result was displayed on different pages. This interpretation was likewise not confirmed. It was not included in the formal assessment because the original entry point did in fact return different revision values at two points in time; but it was not completely ruled out either, because the missing window was not recorded.

After the failure, the page did not pull adjacent projects in to explain the cause. This restraint was appropriate. The behavior of the Quality Signal Console was already complex enough; external speculation would only turn "two states" into a larger narrative. The old materials retained only this project's test, regression tiering, entry point, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause.

## Field experience with regression tiering

Here, regression tiering was not an abstract label. Once a failed sample came in, the on-call person was asking "can this tier still explain it?" rather than "does the system no longer have any failures?" When the current entry point and old record gave different revision values, the tier assessment was forced to carry two contexts: one was the record from when the original sample appeared, and the other was the entry point read later.

This is also why someone later called the issue "the same object appearing in two states." The wording is not precise, but it captured the operational obstacle at the time: no one could, without overwriting the original incident state, compress the failed sample, recovery result, and current entry point into a single record.

The old record chose to list them side by side rather than merge them. The benefit of listing them side by side was preserving the failure window; the downside was that, without additional explanation, readers would treat the two items as simultaneous facts. In particular, when the recovery page showed a passing fixture boundary while the old record still carried the failed sample, the two states looked as if they were still occurring simultaneously.

Regression tiering was not proven in the materials to be the root cause. It was simply the tier that carried the failed samples. Describing it as "the source of the state divergence" is an overreach; describing it as "completely unrelated" is also untenable. The old postmortem did not make this distinction, so it was long misused as an overly strong troubleshooting lead.

## What the exit conditions were at the time

This round of work originally had its own schedule, maintainer, and exit conditions. The old page's record of the exit conditions resembled a simplified decision: after the fixture boundary recovered, stop retrying continuously, retain the original failure window, and defer attribution until subsequent materials. This decision kept the incident from expanding, but it did not provide a sufficient entry point for long-term record maintenance.

Exiting did not mean "only one state remained." The old document did not make this clear, so later readers connected stopping retries, the appearance of the recovery page, and the end of the schedule into a single event. In fact, the three merely occurred at roughly the same stage.

Not overwriting the original failure window on the post-recovery page was an explicitly adopted protective action at the time. PWPC-010 later followed the same principle as well. This consistency shows that preserving the original record was not accidental; but it does not show that the attribution in the original record was reliable.

The old exit conditions also had an implicit premise: the on-call record could be backfilled into the gap in the current revision. After PWPC-011, this premise still had not been implemented. Once the term expired, the on-call person was no longer shown as the long-term owner, and the alternate address was empty. Therefore, even if someone found the window requiring follow-up from this page, they might still be unable to find the original execution record.

This maintenance breakpoint should be considered separately from technical attribution. It explains why the record was not completed, not why the quality signal dashboard once showed two states.

## Materials available for review

The incident report and attachments are still maintained by db · Quality Signal Board, and the entry point is:

`docs/adj-db/incidents/db-quality-signal-board-two-states-for-one-object.md`

DOC-40 is related material for the exit-window checklist. It can help review the checklist-based work at the time, but it cannot serve as proof on this page of why there were two states. This page treats it only as adjacent navigation.

PWPC-010 is suitable for viewing how the recovery results are presented alongside the original state; PWPC-011 is suitable for viewing unrecorded windows and missing alternate addresses. Neither card provides a root-cause conclusion sufficient to replace the old postmortem.

The results in the attachments will not be reorganized here into a "final state." The original page, recovery page, and unconfirmed items were originally stored separately. If specific time records are recovered in the future, a new supplemental note should be added, clearly stating which revision window it supplements; new content should not be inserted back into the old failure window as if it had already been visible when the incident occurred.

## Old troubleshooting notes, retained rather than deleted

The following are the handling recommendations left along with the postmortem at the time. They contain judgments later proven insufficient, and are retained to explain why the schedule ended after fixture boundary recovery.

> Compare the header contract first. If the current entry point differs from the old record, use the current entry point as the baseline; stop rerunning once the fixture boundary passes. Archive the old page and wait for the on-duty team to fill in the revision timestamps. The dual-state condition should disappear on its own in the next round of regression stratification.

The last sentence has no basis. "Disappear on its own in the next round of regression stratification" was a working hypothesis, not an observed result. The old materials do not record whether it occurred or what change would cause it to occur. This assumption should no longer be treated as an exit condition.

Another old note says: "The current entry point is closer to the facts than the old record." This statement also cannot be inferred from the available materials. The current entry point is merely the entry point visible during one particular read; why it differs from the old record is precisely the problem the incident did not resolve. This sentence is retained because it directly influenced the ordering that placed the recovery results first at the time.

There was also a verbal judgment not included in the formal summary: given that the fixture boundary was restored, the signal instability should merely be sample residue. This likewise was not verified. The fact that both the failed samples and the recovery results were preserved shows that those involved at the time did not want either one to override the other; attributing the instability to residue would, in turn, undermine the necessity of preserving both.

## Confirmable scope of the timeline

| Stage | Verifiable records | Actions taken at the time | What cannot be inferred from this |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial discovery | test produced a failing sample, and the current entry point did not match the old records | Saved the original input and the entry point version | The order in which the two revision entries were written |
| Initial comparison | Differences were observed in the header contract | Established a working hypothesis based on that difference | The header contract was the root cause |
| Recovery phase | The fixture boundary could be restored | Stopped retrying and preserved the failure window | The dual-state condition had already disappeared |
| Subsequent maintenance | The recovery page was kept alongside the original incident state | Did not overwrite the object or the failure window | The current result has complete provenance |
| Follow-up record review | The current revision has an undocumented window | Requested a search for the on-duty records | An alternative entry point has been found |
| Maintenance gap | At expiration, the person on duty was no longer shown as the long-term owner, and the replacement address was left blank | Left in the card and page | The cause of the incident has been explained |

This table only organizes the stages already documented in the materials. It does not fill in the missing parts to create a complete, chronological incident timeline. In particular, there is still no record of how much time elapsed between "Initial discovery" and "Initial comparison", or between the recovery page and the entry point change.

The two historical actions on 2026-02-19 show that the scope of the recovery materials was later redefined: first, the scope was confirmed, and then it was pointed out that the current result had no source attached. They do not explain how the incident unfolded in 2025. The supplementary notes on 2026-03-02 and 2026-03-03 show that the long-term owner information had become invalid and the replacement address was left blank; they also cannot be used to infer the origin of the initial revision retrospectively.

## Still unresolved

The most immediate question is: what point in time does each of the two current revision entries correspond to. The original page left blanks, and no usable execution records were added later to fill them in. Without this part, any conclusions about entry point switching, state synchronization, or sample attribution can only be speculation.

The second question is: why did the unstable signal change. Restoring the fixture boundary provides only a partial result. It does not come with a continuous record that could explain the signal changes, nor does it lend any further support to the assessment about the old version of the header contract.

The third issue is: the source of the recovery results. The addendum for PWPC-010 notes that the current results have no source attached. This means that even if the recovery page still exists, it alone cannot establish which original failure sample the results correspond to.

The fourth issue is not technical, but concerns the lookup path. After PWPC-011, the on-call person whose assignment had expired was no longer listed as the long-term owner, and no replacement address was entered. Later follow-up checks that still rely on this person's name will lead to a blank.

These issues have not been resolved in this draft. This page remains a collection of materials from an old incident, not the current definition of states for the quality signal dashboard. Its value lies in preserving the failure samples rather than letting them disappear after recovery, not rewriting incorrect attribution as a correct conclusion, and not disguising gaps in the record as having been filled.

## The old review's final conclusion

The old review ended with "the fixture boundary has been restored, so the same object's dual states will fade away in subsequent layering". This was the working conclusion at the time, and it is also the part of this page most likely to mislead later readers. versions.body:
# Postmortem: State Inconsistency During Caller Integration Testing

This record began when the same tasks object appeared in two different states at the caller integration-testing entry point. Both lookups used the same current entry point, but returned different current revisions; the old record also did not line up with the later result. The initial problem was not knowing which state to continue adapting the sample calls to. This then affected how integration feedback was archived: the same feedback item mapped to different object states depending on when the lookup was made.

This record preserves the object changes observed during integration testing, without extending the incident to failures in other projects. tasks has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria. This anomaly made those boundaries unstable when reviewing the records, but nothing in the available material indicates that behavior in adjacent projects changed at the same time.

## Sequence of Events

- Started by reviewing the sample calls against the old record. The object state in the old record was still readable, but what was visible on the observation side did not match it.
- The first check through the current entry point returned a current revision. At the time, that result was used as the basis for continuing to assess the adaptation boundary during integration testing.
- A later check of the same entry point returned a different current revision. No record explaining the reason for the change was left between the two results, so the later result cannot simply be treated as display lag from the first check.
- Further retries added no useful information and would instead mix more results of unclear provenance into the incident record, so retries were stopped.
- The original record as it stood at the time was retained at `docs/adj-tasks/incidents/tasks-client-integration-two-states-for-one-object.md`. The recovery page could restore access to the maintenance record, but did not answer why the current revision changed.

The initial assessment was "the observation side is still showing the old record." Once the second entry-point result appeared, that explanation was no longer sufficient: if the only issue were that the old record had not been updated, the current entry point should have consistently pointed to the same revision; instead, the entry point itself returned different results at two points in time. The available material only confirms an inconsistency between the entry-point lookups and the old record. It does not establish which part of the call flow, which adaptation, or which piece of integration feedback introduced the change.

## Scope of Impact

The impact was on actual sample calls for tasks and the integration decisions based on them. Callers could previously use the current entry point to choose the object state to align with. After the entry-point results changed, samples could still be saved, but the adaptation boundary they represented had to be understood in the context of the lookup time. Integration feedback also cannot just say "aligned with the current state," because "current" did not identify a single state during the incident.

Maintenance arrangements were not canceled as a result. Work continued on the original object under its independent schedule, and the maintainer did not change. However, the exit criteria cannot treat "the recovery page is accessible" as evidence that integration testing is back to normal. The recovery page addresses retrieval of the maintenance record; it does not mean the two states have been merged or that the caller has selected an adaptation target again.

## Preservation and Recovery

After retries were stopped, the old record was not overwritten, and the later entry-point result was not used to retroactively fill in the earlier assessment. The retained version is used to review which state the sample calls, adaptation boundaries, and integration feedback each depended on at the time. The immediate benefit is that even if the current entry point changes again, it will still be possible to distinguish "what was observed during the incident" from "what the entry point showed later."

The recovery page currently provides a way to look up the maintenance record again. It cannot recover the missing reason for the change or replace the original record. For callers still in integration testing, the recovered record can only serve as a reference for what was observed during the incident. If they need to make adaptation changes based on it, they should first confirm which lookup returned the revision they are relying on.

## Still Unconfirmed

The reason for the record change is still unknown. In particular, it has not yet been established whether the two current revisions came from different stages of the same object update, or whether the entry point read different states at the two points in time. The available records also do not show whether the old exit-action route was related to this inconsistency. The snapshot of that route should be kept separate from this incident record to avoid combining two issues that still need investigation into a single cause.

If original records from before and after the change become available later, they should be appended to this postmortem, with an explanation of which entry-point lookup each corresponds to. Without that material, the conclusion remains: the same tasks object showed different states at two points in time, the maintenance record can be recovered, and the reason for the change has not been confirmed.

# Caller Integration Window Exit Checklist

This page preserves the record of a caller integration window that has already ended. At closure, checks covered only the exit actions, the last visible result, and adj-tasks's own recorded exit actions; whether the release succeeded still required separate sign-off from the relevant owner. It was once used as a short handoff checklist, so the old fields and incomplete recovery records were not cleared out.

The original entry point is still `docs/adj-tasks/release/tasks-client-integration-exit-window-checklist.md`. It holds export records for tasks-client-integration; this page uses it only as a starting point for finding the materials for this window. Someone previously extracted `compatibility` from a similarly named record, but later found that the same term also appeared in older integration notes, so this field alone cannot confirm the window's closure criteria. When reviewing the window, first find the original input, the version record from that time, and the first visible result. If any of the three is missing, all you can do is leave the gap in the window record.

This checklist has always had a narrow scope: actual call samples, adaptation boundaries, and integration feedback relating to tasks. It does not decide releases for other projects or turn a log excerpt into release sign-off. It can still be referenced after the window closes because people handling handoffs often use the last result and the removal actions to cross-check—not because it contains complete integration instructions.

## Capture samples in this order when closing the window

1. [ ] Put the original input, the version record visible at the time, and the first visible result in one place. "First" here means the first result seen after rechecking began for this window, not a green status compiled later. If the original input is no longer available, record the gap and stop; do not substitute another similar call. If the original input and the visible result are stored separately, at least explain the relationship between the two locations in the handoff text; otherwise, the next person can only guess from the filenames whether they belong to the same window.

2. [ ] Keep one sample each of the project's own success path and rejection path. The success path only shows that the call was not rejected at the step being checked; the rejection path is used to confirm that the original integration boundary can still be identified before exit. If the two samples come from different windows, they cannot be presented side by side as the results of a single check. Old records occasionally contain only a success marker. Such a record can show that someone looked at one path at the time, but not that the rejection path was rechecked as well.

3. [ ] Check the artifacts or state left by `push lifecycle`. The old practice treated "success" in the logs as grounds for closing the window. That rule was later crossed out: logs can stay in place, but they do not replace artifacts or state. If the corresponding artifact or state cannot be found, do not check off the exit action. If you find only the wording but no matching call sample, do not move that wording into the "Completed" column either; it may just be a search term left over from early integration notes.

4. [ ] Remove temporary permissions and bypasses, and confirm that the queue is no longer accepting new work. The removal actions and the last visible result must line up. If new call samples still appear after removal, stop the closure process; do not classify this as historical residue. Any accounts, workers, environments, or proxies borrowed during the window must also have a return deadline recorded; items with no stated deadline should not be cleared out along with everything else in the name of "closing the window."

5. [ ] Record the minimum needed for handoff: the location of the last visible result, whether the exit actions are complete, and which sample is missing. Unfinished items should go to a specific person taking over; "The project team will keep an eye on it" is not a substitute for this field. The `operator handoff` in the old record was only a reference keyword left at the time; the actual handoff must still be based on the inputs and results already available for this window.

If ad hoc diagnostics during the window changed the state being investigated, label the post-diagnostic results separately. They can help the person taking over identify what changed, but must not be mixed into the record of results obtained from the original input. The original record reduced this situation to a single line, "Rechecked." That line is still visible, but is no longer considered a sufficient completion marker. If the diagnostics changed the call sample, retain the results from both before and after the change; do not infer one from the other.

## When there are gaps

- Cannot find the paragraph containing `compatibility`: keep the paths you have found and the gap on record; do not fill it in with a configuration block borrowed from another project. A path without the original input still counts as a gap.
- The text `push lifecycle` appears, but there is no corresponding artifact or state: stop at the verification step, and do not record temporary permissions and bypasses as "cleaned up." Logs can remain in place, but cannot replace the missing artifact or state.
- No sample for the rejection path: do not infer from the success path that it still exists; leave this item for the next window in which the original input can be obtained. The handoff only needs to say "No rejection-path sample retained"; there is no need to supply a conclusion for it.
- The queue is still accepting new work after removal: stop closing the window. First retain the call sample being processed at the time and the record of the removal actions, then wait for the relevant owner to decide whether to restore the temporary path.
- Only a green result compiled later remains: do not rewrite it as the first visible result. It can stay as a pointer for later readers, but label it separately from the result seen when rechecking began for the window.

The old version said, "Stop here if `recipient policy` does not appear." That sentence was retained in the previous version because it really was the marker the person on duty used to find materials at the time; however, it did not explain how the term related to the call sample under review, nor did it constitute a release judgment on its own. Later addenda also included `theme mode`, `claim token`, `header contract`, `regression evidence`, `fixture boundary`, and `observability`. These terms are all search tags in the margins of the window record; they do not mean that each item has passed its checks, and should not be treated as general exit criteria.

A recovery procedure was never added to this checklist. Recovery actions that have not been tried in the shared environment remain unconfirmed. If rollback is needed, first retain the records from before and after removal and the call sample being processed, then have the relevant owner decide whether to restore the temporary path. If no pre-recovery result was retained at the time, this page can only state that recovery was not verified; it cannot declare on behalf of the person taking over that the queue or bypass has returned to its original state.

# Release Freeze FAQ

This page is still included in the freeze materials because it records a common misunderstanding: treating a call name that can be found as proof that a candidate path has been closed out. The entry point only lets people return to the same place to investigate and keeps the discussion within the named candidate paths; it does not guarantee the public response or show that regression evidence has been recorded. During the later review, the entry point still worked, but no response conclusion was added on that basis. If all that remains in the freeze table is a call name, treat it as a lead for further investigation, not a reason to close.

**Who is responsible for withdrawing a candidate path?**

The old page assigned withdrawal to the person who proposed the call name, to avoid leaving entries on the list indefinitely. That division did not preserve role boundaries: the person who proposed a name may not be able to judge whether the path is still in use. The available materials do not provide a new ownership mapping, so "the initiator withdraws it" cannot be presented as a universal rule. If no one confirms a candidate path, keeping it is closer to how things were handled at the time than deleting it without authorization; this is also what makes the old table easy to misread.

**Under what conditions can a card be closed?**

The team later continued to use this wording: "A card closes only when the public response, regression evidence, and on-call recovery note agree on the same behavior." This requires the three artifacts to agree on the same behavior, not merely for each of the three to have appeared at some point. The old version treated a single runnable push as a signal to close, which conflicts with this wording; that old judgment remains in the historical answers above.

When the contract diff is missing, some ask whether the entry point and run records can replace it. There is no answer here; it can only be recorded as unknown. DOC-50 records a different single-variable rerun and should not be used to fill the gaps in these three artifacts.
**Can we freeze first if the contract diff is missing?**

The available materials do not provide a universal answer. The entry-point record shows where to continue investigating, and the run record shows that a path was usable on one occasion; neither can replace the missing contract diff. In this situation, the old table would leave a row marked unconfirmed rather than treat "no objections" as approval. This gap remains open here, leaving the actual freeze record to explain why it is waiting or who will supply the evidence.

**What if the three artifacts have different timestamps?**

First, confirm whether they still describe the same behavior. If the recovery note is later than the regression evidence, it only shows that a recovery action was taken afterward; it cannot automatically rewrite the earlier failure. If the public response comes from another candidate path, it cannot be combined with this card to satisfy the closure conditions either. If they cannot be aligned, keep the card open and retain the original timestamp in each artifact, without retrospective corrections.

This page retains only the questions and the short answers supportable at the time; it does not assign owners to specific freeze cards.
